title: A Galaxy With No Stars At All?
hook: Cloud-9 moves like a galaxy but shows no starlight. The deepest images yet — ten times deeper than before — still find nothing, strengthening the case for a galaxy made almost purely of dark matter.
key_points: Cloud-9 is a candidate dark galaxy: a gas cloud that behaves as though it sits in a dark matter halo.
HiPERCAM on the Gran Telescopio Canarias reached surface brightness limits of 31.4 and 31.0 mag/arcsec-squared.
That is roughly ten times deeper than previous imaging of the same field.
No stellar emission appears in the central region, about 1.3 by 1.3 kiloparsecs across.
Assuming an old, metal-poor population, the total stellar mass is under 16,000 solar masses.
Integrated-light limits complement earlier star-count limits, using an independent method.
content_html: Galaxies are usually found by their light. That makes a "dark galaxy" — a cloud of gas held together by a dark matter halo that never lit up — both a natural prediction of structure formation and a nightmare to confirm. You cannot detect it; you can only fail to detect stars in it, ever more convincingly.
extra_html:
Ignacio Trujillo and colleagues went after Cloud-9, the best-known candidate, with HiPERCAM on the 10.4-metre Gran Telescopio Canarias. Their images reach surface-brightness limits of 31.4 mag/arcsec-squared in g and 31.0 in r — roughly ten times deeper than previous work on the field — and find no stellar emission at all across the central arcminute, about 1.3 kiloparsecs on a side.

Translated into mass, and assuming any stars present would be old and metal-poor, that means a stellar surface density no greater than about 0.01 solar masses per square parsec and a total stellar mass under 16,000 solar masses. The result matters partly because of the method: earlier limits came from counting individual resolved stars, while this one comes from integrated light. Two techniques with different failure modes now agree, which is how a candidate slowly turns into a confirmed one.

related.title: Dark Matter & Dark Energy
related.hook: Everything we can see — stars, planets, people — is only about 5% of the universe. The other 95% is two mysteries we've never directly detected.

related.title: Cluster Collisions as Dark Matter Labs
related.hook: Smash two galaxy clusters together and the gas gets stuck while the dark matter sails through. How far it sails is a direct measurement of whether dark matter interacts with itself.

related.title: A Single Star, Magnified a Thousandfold, Maps Invisible Dark Matter
related.hook: Gravity can magnify one ordinary star a thousandfold — and the flicker pattern as it drifts behind a galaxy cluster's lens encodes clues about dark matter clumps invisible any other way.

related.title: Early Galaxies May Be Hiding Most of Their Mass in Faint Stars
related.hook: JWST finds far more small, dim stars in massive early galaxies than expected — enough to make some of them three to four times heavier than we thought, and even harder to explain.

flashcards.prompt: What would a starless galaxy be, and why does it matter?
flashcards.back_html: A gas cloud sitting in its own dark matter halo that never managed to form stars. It would be a dark matter structure you can weigh without any starlight confusing the picture.

flashcards.prompt: Why is this non-detection stronger evidence than earlier searches?

choices.text: The images go about ten times deeper in surface brightness, and use integrated light rather than resolved star counts
It used a space telescope instead of a ground-based one
It measured the cloud's rotation rather than its brightness

flashcards.explanation_html: Depth plus an independent method: integrated light and resolved-star counts fail in different ways, so agreement between them is more convincing than either alone.

flashcards.prompt: What does a surface-brightness limit like 31 mag/arcsec-squared actually buy you?
flashcards.back_html: It converts into a cap on stellar mass — here under about 16,000 solar masses for an old, metal-poor population. Fainter limit, tighter cap on hidden stars.
